newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Imatron to slow expansion.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Imatron to slow expansion.

text.p: Imatron Inc will dramatically slow its planned expansion this year so it can focus instead on boosting public awareness on the benefits of its Ultrafast scanner, President and Chief Excutive Officer S. Lewis Meyer said Wednesday.

Although the Ultrafast scanner has been widely endorsed by cardiologists as one of the best non-invasive ways to detect hardening of the arteries, that message has been slow to reach the general public and insurers, he said.
Meyer said Imatron now plans to open just one new HeartScan imaging center this year, down from earlier plans to open 12.

"We will not open more centers until we have broken the code of how to center profitability," he said. "Realistically, I think it will take another year to crack some of the big insurers. Some of them do cover the (Ultrafast scanning test), but a lot of the big ones still do not."
In addition to slowing its expansion, Meyer said Imatron may seek a corporate partnership to help it launch a nationwide campaign promoting the scanner's benefits.

The Ultrafast scanner takes images of the heart and arteries at a rate about 20 times faster than X-ray imaging. As a result, it produces far clearer pictures that are not distorted by the heart's own beating motion.

The product has been on the market for about five years, but it got a boost a year ago when a study suggested it was the best way available to detect the early stages of heart disease. The study recommended it be used routinely the way mammograms are routinely used to check for breast cancer.
Wall Street initially embraced that concept, but later soured when the Ultrafast scanner proved slow to catch on.
Imatron's stock closed Wednesday at 2-21/32, down from a high for the year of more than $6. Last year, shortly after the company embarked on an aggressive expansion plan, its share price topped $7.

Today, Imatron has about 100 scanners on the market and four HeartScan scanning centers, in Houston, Pittsburg, Seattle and Washington D.C. The new center planned for this year will be located in New York City.
With a scan costing about $400, Meyer said many patients have been reluctant to undergo this procedure without reimbursement from their insurers.

But he said the scanner will ultimately save money by identifying patients at risk for heart disease. The company says such patients can reduce their risk, if they are aware of it, by going on drugs that reduce cholesterol.
"We certainly expected to expand more rapidly," Meyer said. "It's just a matter of getting the message out, which is not easy for a small company like Imatron to do."
